name: Weight cycling (bulk-cut)

lead: Bulk-cut cycling means spending a period eating above maintenance to add muscle (and some fat), then a period eating below maintenance to lose fat while keeping the muscle.

The payoff is a bigger, leaner physique: lifters add size in the surplus and show definition after the deficit. Bodybuilders typically bulk in an off-season and cut around 12 to 14 weeks before a show.

paras: Lifters track body weight and calories, run a surplus during bulks (clean or dirty), then a deficit during cuts, with resistance training throughout. Some use lean bulks or maintenance breaks to limit fat gain.

Larger surpluses add more fat. Observational data link weight fluctuation to poorer health outcomes, but a 2026 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology review judged evidence does not support causal harm from cycling itself. Extreme water cuts in combat sports raise separate concerns.

angle.text: Bulking adds the muscle and cutting reveals it, so repeated cycles are used to build a larger, leaner physique over time.

lead: Weight cycling in lifting culture is the deliberate alternation of bulking and cutting. A bulk is a calorie surplus to build muscle; a cut is a calorie deficit to lose fat while holding muscle.[1]

Bodybuilders usually bulk through the off-season and begin cutting about 12 to 14 weeks before a show. A "clean bulk" tracks macros to limit fat gain, while a "dirty bulk" uses a large, loosely tracked surplus that adds fat quickly and usually calls for a harder cut.[1] Looksmaxxing forums discuss timing of bulk and cut phases.[2]

Outside lifting, repeated loss and regain is called yo-yo dieting. A 2024 review of 23 studies found most showed no significant association with weight, fat mass increases, lean mass loss or metabolic rate changes,[3] and a 2026 review concluded evidence does not support a causal link to clinical harm.[4] Other sources note correlational links to higher mortality, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.[5]

paras: Bulking is eating in a surplus; larger surpluses or longer bulks tend to add more fat alongside muscle. Cutting is a deficit; a larger deficit loses weight faster but risks muscle loss.[1]
The 1950s and 1960s saw "bulking up" and "cutting down" nutrition popularised via bodybuilding magazines and physique contests.[1]
A looksmax.org thread titled "When do you Bulk/Cut?" shows members discussing when to switch phases.[2]

Reviews of yo-yo dieting describe a public perception that it raises fat and lowers metabolism; a 2024 systematic review found most studies did not show this.[3] A 2026 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology piece concluded evidence does not support causal clinical harm, attributing observed adverse associations to circumstantial factors.[4] A general overview cites correlational links of weight fluctuation to mortality, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.[5]
Reviews of weight loss in combat sports and wrestling document rapid weight-cutting practices and their concerns.[6][7]
Studies of weight cycling in general populations exist (see above), but none specifically test lifters' bulk-cut cycles.[3][4]

lore.intro: Lifters on forums discuss bulk and cut timing as a core planning question.[2]
